facts.note: Paper §7.1 (p6) states 'Debt rescheduling opportunities have been limited due to the level of premium (penalty) that would be chargeable by the PWLB and LOBO providers. summary.text:
Royal Borough of Greenwich's Treasury Management and Capital Outturn 2025-26 (19 pages) was taken as Item 14 at Council on 22 July 2026, the final decision meeting after Cabinet (15 July 2026) and Audit and Risk Management Panel (21 July 2026). The paper is authored by Michael Horbatchewskyj, Jason Coniam and Julian Gocool (Accountancy Business Change Manager), reporting to Andrew Vallance (Interim Assistant Director of Finance); Chief Officer for the paper is Damon Cook (Director of Resources). The substantive treasury figures sit in the covering report itself (Tables 1-3 and Charts 1-2 cover the loan book, CFR, borrowing walk, maturity profile and investment outturn), which is enough to reconcile the loan book and check the balance-sheet identity. Appendix A (Treasury Management Indicators and Limits) is listed at §19.1 as attached but is not present in this PDF — the schedule of Authorised Limit, Operational Boundary, actual maturity structure limits, financing cost ratio and >365-day investment upper limit sits separately, so observations on prudential-indicator headroom are constrained to what §10.1 states in narrative (that all limits were complied with). The S151 officer is referred to in the Legal implications block but not named in this paper.

The loan book reconciles cleanly. Our file, pulled under the exact bc-loans name “ROYAL BOROUGH OF GREENWICH” (“Greenwich Council” and “Royal Greenwich” would not match), holds 56 individual PWLB advances totalling £805,490,477 at a coupon-weighted 4.2748% (49 MATURITY-profile plus 7 EIP). Table 1 (p3) prints PWLB principal £805.490m at 4.27% weighted, described as fixed-rate maturity loans. Principal ties to £477 on rounding; rate ties to two decimal places (4.2748% rounds to 4.27%). The year's PWLB net movement also ties: our file walks from £625,907k at 31 March 2025 to £805,490k at 31 March 2026 (+£179,583k), and §5.1 (p3) discloses £235m new PWLB drawn less £55.4m historical PWLB repaid (+£179.6m). Textbook reconciliation.

The single most distinctive figure in the report is at the very foot of Table 1: the residual weighted duration of the debt portfolio fell from 20 years (24/25) to 13.4 years (25/26) — a 6.6-year drop in one financial year, on a book that grew by £175m. That is not accidental. §6.3 narrates the policy: the Council “sought to minimise the taking on of long-term borrowing at elevated levels and has focused on a policy of Internal and temporary borrowing, supplemented by short term borrowing”. §6.4 signals what follows: “the primary focus of the Council borrowing strategy will shift to external borrowing, as the balance sheet resource available to borrow against is estimated to decrease”. The council-year captured in this outturn is when the shift began: £235m of new PWLB was drawn, deliberately at shorter maturities than the existing book, to avoid locking in what §6.6 describes as “elevated” long rates through 2025/26. Weighted rate on the book is essentially unchanged (4.24% → 4.23%), so the shortening was achieved without raising the weighted coupon. Our maturity snapshot at 15 August 2026 (53 live loans, £758.6m — £46.9m has already come off since 31 March 2026) puts £470.2m or 62.0% of the PWLB book inside 5 years, with the £335.4m 2-5y bucket the dominant concentration.

The balance-sheet identity ties at the aggregate level only. Table 2 (p5) prints CFR at 31 March 2026 of £1,214,752k against external debt of £907,932k. CFR less external gives £306,820k, which matches the paper's printed “Under/(Over) Borrowing” of £306,820k to the pound. The paper does not disclose Other Long-Term Liabilities (PFI/finance leases) separately, so this £306.8m aggregate cannot be split into internal borrowing and OLTL from this report alone. Greenwich almost certainly carries some OLTL; the split would sit in the Statement of Accounts (a separate document on the same July committee cycle — audited accounts, doc 20255/20256, not read under session instruction). The full identity CFR − external borrowing − OLTL = internal borrowing therefore ties in aggregate but not in decomposition. Direction-of-travel per §6.4 is that the aggregate under-borrow will fall as reserves deplete and the balance-sheet resource contracts, forcing more external borrowing.

Three other observations. First, LOBOs fell £5.0m in the year (£44.5m → £39.5m) with no narrative comment on cause — possibly a call refused with borrower repayment, a call accepted, or scheduled amortisation. Cannot attribute from this paper. Second, investment balances rose £31m (£46m → £77m) as cash was held forward against near-term capital deployment even as external debt grew £175m; yield fell 90bp to 4.02% as Bank Rate cuts through the year (4.50% → 3.75%) and a deliberate liquidity-first stance into DMADF and call accounts drove the mix. Third, on the DMO's premature repayment curve dated 14 August 2026 our engine prices the live PWLB book at a net indicative discount of £44.8m (6.0% of £751.2m priced balance), with 25 loans below par and 28 above. The single largest discount by a wide margin is loan 450475 — a £40m 1.37% PWLB maturing 8 December 2071, indicative discount £27.2m or 68% of par. It is the biggest single legacy asset in the book, a pandemic-era certainty-window fixing at less than a third of today's 50y rate, and it is exactly the loan a treasurer would want to keep. Do not surface as any kind of rescheduling suggestion. §7.1 (p6) says rescheduling was not undertaken because premium (penalty) would be chargeable — correct on the repay-and-reborrow frame, and our engine gives the same answer on that test. Unlike Devon and Somerset FRA and East Sussex FRA, this paper does not explicitly open the repay-without-reborrow frame, so the discount finding has less textual anchor here than it does elsewhere.

Rate view tested. §6.7 (p4) reports that at start of April 2026 the market expected Bank Rate to move UP to 4.00% or 4.25% from 3.75%. That expectation has not materialised: Bank Rate at 14 August 2026 is 3.75% — unchanged from the April anchor for the full four months since. §6.6 says Bank Rate reduced to 3.75% during 2025/26 “as anticipated”, which Table 3 (p7) confirms independently. Bank Rate call landed to the point. On the long end, the paper does not print its own current-day PWLB curve for direct match, so no rate-to-rate check is available in the outturn.

Email drafted per session instruction. The strongest hook is the duration-halving story: the reconciliation earns the credit, then the 20 → 13.4 year duration shift as the visible print-out of the strategy §6.3 narrates. Recipient question is open: the S151 is not named in this paper. Damon Cook (Director of Resources) is Chief Officer for the paper and would be the reasonable primary recipient; Andrew Vallance (Interim Assistant Director of Finance) is the direct reporting officer and would be a defensible alternative primary; and the three report authors (Michael Horbatchewskyj, Jason Coniam and Julian Gocool) are the operational contacts. All five addresses are printed at §20 (p19). Draft addresses Damon Cook as primary with Andrew Vallance and the three authors on Cc, and takes every title verbatim from the paper without labelling anyone S151.

officer.body:
Damon,

Apologies for the cold email — PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're a small platform that carries PWLB rates at both daily fixings, monthly local-authority-to-local-authority lending activity, every borrower's PWLB loan book priced daily against the DMO's premature repayment curve, and a lightweight academy for treasury officers and members. All of the data side is free and stays free. There's more in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL] if it helps to circulate.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that read committee papers across every authority in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. Below are a few thoughts on your 22 July outturn paper, offered ahead of the mid-year 2026/27 review to Audit and Risk Management Panel later in the autumn. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The outturn is unusually well-scoped for a 19-page document, with the loan-book table and the CFR walk both landing on the first six pages, and this is offered in that spirit rather than as a critique.

The reconciliation earns the rest. Our own file, pulled from the DMO borrower schedule under "ROYAL BOROUGH OF GREENWICH" (not "Greenwich Council" or "Royal Greenwich", which are naming quirks we ran into), holds fifty-six individual PWLB advances totalling £805,490,477 at a coupon-weighted 4.2748%. Your Table 1 prints PWLB principal at £805.490m at 4.27% weighted, described as fixed-rate maturity loans. Principal ties to £477 on rounding, and the rate ties to two decimal places. The year's PWLB net movement also ties: our file walks £625,907k at 31 March 2025 to £805,490k at 31 March 2026, an increase of £179,583k, against paragraph 5.1's £235m new less £55.4m repaid, net £179.6m. It's a clean reconciliation and it means anything else we say below is grounded in the same fifty-six loans you are working from.

The most distinctive figure in the outturn sits at the very foot of Table 1: the residual weighted duration of the debt portfolio fell from 20 years last year to 13.4 years this year — 6.6 years off the book in a single financial year, on a book that grew by £175m. That is not accidental. Paragraph 6.3 narrates the policy exactly: the Council "sought to minimise the taking on of long-term borrowing at elevated levels and has focused on a policy of Internal and temporary borrowing, supplemented by short term borrowing". The £235m of new PWLB drawn in the year was deliberately weighted short of the existing book, and the weighted rate barely moved (4.24% to 4.23%) so the shortening was achieved without raising the weighted coupon. In our maturity buckets at 15 August 2026 the 2-5 year range now holds £335m at 4.36% — the visible print-out of that year's borrowing. Your loan book, sliced by contract maturity and by LOBO next-call date, is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis if it is useful to have alongside.

On the balance-sheet identity. Your Table 2 prints CFR at £1,214,752 and external debt at £907,932; £1,214,752 less £907,932 is £306,820, which matches your "Under/(Over) Borrowing" line to the pound. The one thing we cannot do from the outturn alone is decompose the £306.8m into internal borrowing and Other Long-Term Liabilities — the outturn does not carry the PFI or finance-lease figure so the two are combined in the printed "Under/(Over)" number. Nothing turns on this for the identity check, which ties; it is just a note that if the Statement of Accounts publishes the OLTL split we would apply the full identity to it and it would sit at the pound as well.

On the LOBO line. Table 1 shows LOBOs down £5m in the year, from £44.5m to £39.5m, with no narrative on cause. The pattern across the councils we have read this year is that LOBO calls in this rate environment have overwhelmingly been refused — twelve refused calls we've logged so far, with a small number handled through borrower repayment or a new floating structure instead. Whether the £5m came off through a call, negotiated repayment or amortisation is not visible in the outturn — kept as an observation. Our monthly LA-to-LA and LOBO activity page is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

A note on where the paper's rate view has travelled. Paragraph 6.6 says Bank Rate cut to 3.75% "as anticipated", which Table 3 confirms independently — the Bank Rate call landed to the point. Paragraph 6.7 records that at the start of April 2026 the market expected Bank Rate to move up to 4.00% or 4.25% from 3.75%. That expectation has not materialised: Bank Rate at today's DMO fixing (14 August 2026) is still 3.75%, unchanged for the four months since. That is context on where the paper's April 2026 anchor sits against actual, not a critique of the strategy — the flat outturn is arguably a helpful backdrop to the shorter-weighted new borrowing rather than a challenge to it. The daily curve and the derived liability benchmark page are at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity, and CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates put the liability benchmark in front of every S151 this cycle, so having a version that moves with the market rather than being recalculated annually is worth a look.

A disclosure on our own coverage. We hold PWLB only. Your Table 1 shows £805.490m of PWLB out of £907.932m total external debt — so we hold 89% of your external book, and the reconciliation above is on the PWLB portion; the £52.5m fixed bank loan, £39.5m of LOBOs, £1.62m green fund and £8.82m street-lighting AMBER loan sit outside what we hold. Investment positions and counterparty tables also sit outside.

One observation on the shape of the book, framed carefully. On the DMO's premature repayment curve today our engine prices the live PWLB book at a net indicative discount of £44.8m across the fifty-three loans still live (6.0% of the £751m priced balance, with twenty-five loans below par and twenty-eight above). The single largest discount by a wide margin sits on one loan — the £40m at 1.37% maturing 8 December 2071 — which prices at an indicative £27.2m discount, or 68% of par, precisely because the coupon is so far below today's 50-year rate of 6.27%. That is the biggest legacy asset in the book and it is exactly the loan a treasurer would want to keep — a pandemic-era certainty-window fixing that would never be replaced on today's curve. Recorded here as an observation on the shape of the book, not as a rescheduling suggestion. Paragraph 7.1 states that rescheduling was not undertaken because the premium would be chargeable, and on the repay-and-reborrow test our engine gives the same answer. Indicative only — the DMO's quote is the only binding one, we model no MRP effect and no accounting treatment.

On training, three courses would fit here — a Liability Benchmark session pitched at a book of your scale, one on premature repayment and rescheduling arithmetic that covers the mechanics behind paragraph 7.1, and a Prudential and Treasury Code refresher for the mid-year cycle. Everything is free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

If any of this is useful, word of mouth is how we reach colleagues at other authorities — a mention to a peer treasurer in London does more than any campaign we could run.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
